```c
while(1) {
    char *line = buffer;
    int line_len = buffer_len;

    while(((line = fgets(line, line_len, fd)) != NULL)
          && strlen(line) > 0
          && (line[strlen(line) - 1] != '\n')) {
      i = strlen(line);
      old_buffer = buffer;
      old_buffer_len = buffer_len;
      buffer_len += chunk_len;

      buffer = ndpi_realloc(old_buffer, old_buffer_len, buffer_len);
      if(buffer == NULL) {
        NDPI_LOG_ERR(ndpi_str, "Memory allocation failure\n");
        ndpi_free(old_buffer);
        return -2;
      }

      line = &buffer[i];
      line_len = chunk_len;
    } /* while */
```

The key bug: `line = &buffer[i]` where `i = strlen(line)`. On the second iteration, `line` points to `&buffer[first_chunk_len]`. Then `i = strlen(&buffer[first_chunk_len])` = length of the second chunk. Then `line = &buffer[second_chunk_len]`.

So on the third iteration, `line = &buffer[second_chunk_len]`. If the second chunk is short, `line` points near the beginning of the buffer. `fgets` then reads into `buffer[second_chunk_len..second_chunk_len+1022]`.

But here's the critical issue: `fgets` reads at most `line_len - 1 = 1023` characters. If `line = &buffer[1]` (second_chunk_len = 1), then `fgets` reads up to 1023 chars into `buffer[1..1023]`. The buffer is at least 2048 bytes. So this is within bounds.

BUT - what if `fgets` reads MORE than `line_len - 1` characters? Let me check the glibc `fgets` implementation.

Actually, let me look at this from a different angle. The crash is "Heap-buffer-overflow READ 2". This is a READ, not a WRITE. So the overflow happens when reading from the buffer, not writing to it.

Where do we read from the buffer?
1. `strlen(line)` - reads 1 byte at a time
2. `line[strlen(line) - 1]` - reads 1 byte
3. `strlen(buffer)` - reads 1 byte at a time
4. `buffer[i - 1]` - reads 1 byte
5. `buffer[i-1] == '\r'` - reads 1 byte
6. `ndpi_handle_rule(ndpi_str, buffer)` - reads from buffer

The READ 2 suggests a 2-byte read. This could be from `strlen` if it's optimized to read 2 bytes at a time (e.g., using word-at-a-time optimization).

Let me think about when `strlen` could read past the end of the buffer. `strlen(buffer)` reads from `buffer[0]` until it finds a null byte. If the buffer has no null byte within its allocated size, `strlen` reads past the end.

When does the buffer have no null byte? After the inner while loop exits, the last `fgets` call null-terminates the buffer. But where does it place the null byte?

If the last `fgets` call reads `n` characters (where `n < line_len - 1`), it places a null byte at `line[n]`. If `line = &buffer[offset]`, then the null byte is at `buffer[offset + n]`.

But `strlen(buffer)` reads from `buffer[0]`. If `buffer[0..offset+n-1]` has no null bytes, then `strlen(buffer)` reads up to `buffer[offset+n]` where the null byte is. This is within bounds.

BUT - what if `offset + n` exceeds the buffer size? Let me think...

`offset` is `i` from the previous iteration, which is `strlen(line)` from the previous chunk. `n` is the number of chars read by the last `fgets`. 

If the previous chunk was 1023 chars, then `offset = 1023`. If the last `fgets` reads 1023 chars (no newline found), then `n = 1023`. The null byte is at `buffer[1023 + 1023] = buffer[2046]`. The buffer is at least 2048 bytes (after the first realloc). So `buffer[2046]` is within bounds.
